You make guesses about the present and the past with the future and conditional of probability (será, estará, habrá sido, tendría) and other expressions of hypothesis (a lo mejor, quizás, puede que + subjunctive).
to keep one’s feet on the ground
Who can A. be? — It must be Andrés.
He must be about ninety now.
He must have closed the bookshop because of the crisis.
It must have been three in the morning when she left.
To make guesses about the present with the simple future (será, estará, tendrá).
To make guesses about the recent past with the future perfect (habrá sido, habrá cerrado).
To make guesses about the past with the conditional (serían las tres, tendría veinte años).
To choose the right mood after a lo mejor, quizás, puede que, debe de.

The next morning, in a café near Piața Romană. Ecaterina has put the novel on the table, open at the dedication. Ana came as soon as she could. Costel, who is passing through Bucharest, has come too, still in his work clothes.
Look. At the end of the dedication, in very small letters, there’s an initial: “A.”. I didn’t see it yesterday. My glasses must have been dirty.
It must be Andrés. Who else could it be?
Don’t get your hopes up, my girl. It could be anyone else. There must be hundreds of names starting with A.
But the author grew up in her grandfather’s bookshop, in the same neighbourhood. That can’t be a coincidence.
Andrés was a widower when I met him. He had a teenage daughter, Pilar. Maybe Marta is Pilar’s daughter.
Then Marta would be his granddaughter. And he must be… how old now?
In 1977 he must have been about forty. So now he must be nearly ninety. If he’s alive.
And why wouldn’t he have looked for you all these years?
I don’t know. He may have started a new life. Or he may have been ashamed. Or he may have been angry with me, and rightly so.
There’s a way to find out. I can write to the publisher in Madrid and ask them for Marta’s contact details.
(after a long silence) Write to them. But don’t tell them who I am. Not yet.
“llevaría las gafas sucias” = my glasses must have been dirty
“no te hagas ilusiones” = don’t get your hopes up
“tendría unos cuarenta” = he must have been about forty
“habrá rehecho su vida” = he may have started a new life
All future forms are stressed on the ending, with a written accent: se-RÁ, ten-DRÁ, es-ta-RÁ. Without the accent, “sera” doesn’t even exist.
Guesses are said in a slightly hesitant tone, falling at the end: «Será Andrés…» Often with «supongo», «digo yo».
Silent h, stress on the last syllable: a-BRÁ.
1. The future of probability: guesses about the present
In Spanish, the simple future may have nothing to do with the future: it expresses a guess about NOW. In English: “must”, “probably”, “I suppose”.
It must be Andrés. / It’s probably Andrés.
I wonder what time it is.
To answer a question with “será”, you can also use the future: «¿Dónde está Ana? — Estará en clase.» (She must be in class.)
2. The future perfect and the conditional: guesses about the past
past linked to the present (perfecto → future perfect)
past of the past (pluscuamperfecto → conditional perfect)
Careful: here the conditional does NOT mean “would”: «Serían las tres» = “It must have been three o’clock”, not “it would be three o’clock”.
A lo mejor Marta es su nieta.
Puede que sea cualquier otra persona.
Debe de tener casi noventa años.

“Deber de” = probability; “deber” (without de) = obligation. «Debe de estar en casa» (He must be at home – I suppose) versus «Debe estar en casa» (He has to be at home). In speech many Spaniards mix them up, but in the exam keep them apart.
From certainty to doubt: Es seguro que… → Seguramente… → Será… → A lo mejor… → Puede que… → Es poco probable que…
¿Qué hay al final de la dedicatoria?
Escribir a la editorial de Madrid
A news story about a mystery in a museum. Notice how the journalists make guesses.
An anonymous painting, forgotten for decades in the storeroom of a museum in Toledo, could be the work of a great seventeenth-century painter, according to several experts.
“They must have put it there by mistake during some renovation,” explains the museum’s director. “In those days there were no digital inventories and many things got lost.”
Nobody knows how the painting reached the museum. Some noble family probably donated it at the beginning of the twentieth century. The donation documents may still be in some archive.
The analyses will take several months. Meanwhile, the painting will be on display to the public, although unsigned and with a very cautious label: “Masterpiece or copy? You decide.”
En el almacén de un museo de Toledo

Ana wrote to the publisher in Madrid that same afternoon. It was a short, cautious email, as Ecaterina had asked. She explained that she was a Spanish teacher in Bucharest, that a Romanian translator was working on Marta Gil’s novel and that she had some questions about the text. She asked, if possible, for the author’s contact details. She mentioned neither the dedication, nor the year 1987, nor Ecaterina’s name.
Then the waiting began. And as always happens when you wait, everyone started making guesses.

Costel, who was back on the road, sent messages from every motorway service area in Central Europe. “Have they answered? They probably haven’t read the email yet. They must be on holiday. What time must it be in Madrid now, in October? The same as Bucharest minus one, right?” Ana answered patiently, although sometimes she was a bit slow, because she was teaching.

One night, from a car park near Linz, Costel sent a longer message than usual. He said he had done some calculations: if the bookseller was forty in 1977, he would be nearly ninety now; if he was alive, he must be retired; and if he was retired, he must have plenty of free time to read emails. “So he’ll answer,” he concluded. “And if he doesn’t answer, there must be a reason. And if there’s a reason, we’ll find it.” Ana thought Costel would have made a good detective.

Andrei, the club’s young photographer, decided that this kind of waiting was too slow for his generation. That same evening he found Marta Gil’s profile on a social network. She had few posts, almost all of them photos of books. But there was one that made him stop: an old man seen from behind, sitting on a bench in the Retiro park, with a cap and an open book on his knees. Underneath, a single sentence: “My first reader”.

Andrei sent the photo to Ana at eleven at night. Ana looked at it for a long time. You couldn’t see his face. He could be any old man in Madrid. But something in the way he held the book, with his left hand open underneath like a tray, seemed strangely familiar. She decided not to show it to Ecaterina until she was sure. She didn’t want to get her hopes up.

A week went by. Then another. The publisher didn’t reply. In class, the B2 group happened to be studying the future of probability, and the exercises in the book began to seem written for the occasion. “Why wouldn’t she have answered?”, “She must be very busy”, “She must have lost the email”, the students repeated, and then glanced sideways at Ecaterina.

Aunt Viorica, who had heard everything from Andrei, had her own theory, and she set it out one Sunday at lunch, her spoon in the air. According to her, the bookseller would have married someone else, would have ten grandchildren and wouldn’t remember a thing. “Men forget quickly,” she declared. Then, with a dangerous gleam in her eye, she suggested telling the story live to her hundred and twenty thousand followers. “I’m sure one of them in Madrid knows him,” she said. Ana strictly forbade her to touch her phone until dessert.

Mihai, on the other hand, had a doctor’s hypothesis, and he didn’t dare say it out loud in front of anyone. A man of nearly ninety who stops writing, closes his bookshop and suddenly asks his granddaughter to write down his memories… That usually meant one thing: that his memories were slipping away. He told only Ana, at night, in a whisper. Ana didn’t answer. She had been thinking exactly the same thing for days.

Ecaterina, for her part, behaved as if nothing was happening. She arrived on time, corrected the others’ mistakes with her usual severity and in the afternoons kept translating the novel, page after page. She had already translated five chapters. But Ana noticed that she had started keeping her bag always closed and pressed against her body, and she suspected why: the letter was inside.

One Thursday after class, Ecaterina asked Ana to stay for a moment. She opened the novel at page 112 and pointed to a paragraph. In the novel, a young Romanian woman walked into a bookshop on a rainy day looking for a book by Cortázar. The bookseller, a tall man with round glasses, recommended another book. She said she didn’t want it. He gave it to her anyway.
“That happened,” Ecaterina said quietly. “Exactly like that. The book was One Hundred Years of Solitude. I still have it. Nobody but him could know that detail. Nobody. I didn’t even tell my mother.”
“Then his granddaughter knows because he told her,” said Ana.

“Or because he wrote it, and she only signed the book,” Ecaterina replied. “At this point, I don’t know what to think any more. He may be alive. He may have died years ago and left his notebooks. It may all be an impossible coincidence.”

That was when Ana decided to show her the photo of the old man on the bench in the Retiro. Ecaterina put on her glasses, wiped them with the end of her scarf, put them back on and looked at the phone screen for a whole minute without saying anything. Then she touched the screen with one finger, right above the old man’s left hand, open under the book like a tray.
“That’s how he read,” she said. “Always. He used to say books weigh less if you carry them the way you carry a plate of hot soup.”

Ana didn’t know what to say. Ecaterina gave her back the phone, got up slowly and went home without saying goodbye. It was the first time in two years she had left class without saying “see you Thursday”.

The next day, Ecaterina didn’t come to class. It was the first time she had missed one without telling anyone. Ana called her three times. She didn’t answer. In the evening, finally, a message arrived: “I’m fine. I spent the day reading One Hundred Years of Solitude again. I hadn’t opened it for forty years. His handwriting is on the first page. I hadn’t dared to look at it until today.” Ana read the message on the bus and had to get off one stop early to breathe.

That night, Ana couldn’t take it any more. She knew Ecaterina had asked her to be cautious, but she also knew that an eighty-year-old woman doesn’t have all the time in the world to be cautious. She opened the social network, found Marta Gil’s profile and wrote her a private message. She wrote it six times. The final version was very short.

“Hello, Marta. My name is Ana and I’m a Spanish teacher in Bucharest. Someone very dear to me is translating your novel into Romanian. Her name is Ecaterina. I think your grandfather may know who she is. If not, I’m sorry to have bothered you.”

She pressed “send” before she could change her mind. Then she switched off her phone, left it in the kitchen next to Carmen’s frying pan, and went to bed. Mihai, half asleep, asked her what she had done. Ana told him she had just opened a door. Mihai mumbled that he hoped it wasn’t the fridge door, and went back to sleep.

In the morning, when Ana switched on her phone, there was a message. It had arrived at twenty past four in the morning, Madrid time. She read it standing up in the kitchen, coffee in hand, while Rosa Elena ate cereal for breakfast and told her something about a dinosaur.

“Hello, Ana. I haven’t slept all night. I read your message to my grandfather in the early hours. His name is Andrés Gil. He is eighty-nine. He has lived with me for two years, because he can’t live alone any more. He hardly speaks. Sometimes he doesn’t recognise me. But when I told him Ecaterina’s name, he closed his eyes and said a whole sentence, the first in months: ‘Tell her I still have her Cortázar.’”

“I wrote that novel with his memories, the ones he told me when he could still remember. He asked me for the dedication. The A. is his. He had been waiting forty years for a letter. Do you think she would want to talk to him? I don’t know how much time we have left. Marta.”

Ana put her coffee down on the table. Rosa Elena stopped talking about the dinosaur and looked at her worriedly. “Mummy, why are you crying?” she asked. Ana told her she wasn’t crying, it was the onion. Rosa Elena looked around the kitchen, where there was no onion at all, and decided, with the wisdom of her almost five years, not to ask any more questions.

Ana put her coat on over her pyjamas, grabbed the car keys and set off for Ecaterina’s house. On the way, she thought about how she would tell her. She thought of every possible way to begin. When she finally rang the bell and Ecaterina opened the door, in her dressing gown, with a cup of tea in her hand, Ana realised she wouldn’t need any of them.

Ecaterina looked her in the eyes for three seconds. Then she put the cup down on the hall table, very slowly, like someone putting down something fragile. And she said, in a voice Ana had never heard from her before:
